 The Mahanadi Coalfields IPO Explained
 In today's Finshots, we look at the Mahanadi Coalfields RHP and discuss what its IPO reveals about the future of coal in India.

 The Story
 India's electricity demand is growing rapidly. Apart from more homes getting connected to the grid, people are buying electric vehicles, factories and industries are expanding, and data centres are expanding, too.
 Despite the country's ambitious renewable energy targets, coal continued to supply close to 45% of the country’s installed capacity as of 2025.
 So coal remains the backbone of India's electricity generation, providing the dependable supply that solar and wind cannot always guarantee. And one company sitting right in the middle of this is Mahanadi Coalfields Limited, or MCL, a subsidiary of Coal India. 
 Operating primarily in Odisha's Talcher and Ib Valley coalfields, MCL is India's largest coal producer by volume. In FY26, it produced around 218 million tonnes of coal, accounting for roughly 21% of India's domestic coal output. Its customers include thermal power plants as well as industries such as aluminium, cement and sponge iron.
 Now, MCL is heading to the stock market with a 100% offer for sale (OFS) by its promoter, Coal India Ltd. They are offering up to 661.84 million equity shares with a price band of ₹129-136 per share. And because this is entirely an OFS, MCL itself won't receive any money from the IPO. The proceeds will go to Coal India.
 Which brings us to the question: Why is Coal India offloading its stake in Mahanadi Coal?
 Well, it’s part of Coal India's broader plan to unlock value from its subsidiaries. It has already taken Bharat Coking Coal Limited public in January 2026 and Central Mine Planning & Design Institute Limited in March 2026. But MCL is arguably one of the most important assets in this exercise, given its scale, production volumes and profitability.
 So, on the surface, MCL looks like a fairly straightforward investment in India's coal demand. It has enormous reserves, highly mechanised operations and some of the best productivity numbers in the industry. But there is an important detail investors need to understand before getting carried away: Pricing power. That’s because MCL doesn't have complete freedom over how much it charges for its coal.
 Most of its coal is sold through long-term Fuel Supply Agreements, or FSAs, with power plants and other industrial customers. These base prices for non-coking coal are notified centrally by Coal India, depending on the grade. MCL primarily supplies utility-grade coal, particularly grades G11 to G14. 
 Sidebar: Utility-grade coal refers to coal primarily used by power plants to generate electricity. Coal India classifies non-coking coal into grades G1 to G17 based on the heat it produces when burned. Thermal power plants commonly use these grades, which can burn larger quantities of coal to generate electricity. In FY26, around 82.12% of its product sales came through these long-term agreements, at an average realisation of approximately ₹1,354 per tonne. The remaining 17.88% was sold through electronic auctions, where buyers compete for available coal. These auctions fetched an average realisation of approximately ₹1,797 per tonne.
 Source: Mahanadi Coalfields Ltd RHP That difference is important because e-auctions allow MCL to earn a premium over the notified prices. And when you're selling hundreds of millions of tonnes of coal, even a relatively small change in the premium can have a meaningful impact on profitability.
 Consider what happened between FY24 and FY26. MCL's coal dispatches reached a record 210.74 million tonnes in FY26. Yet its revenue from operations fell from ₹31,634 crore in FY24 to ₹30,550 crore in FY26.
 Source: Mahanadi Coalfields Ltd RHP The reason was the normalisation of auction premiums. In FY24, auction prices were around ₹802 per tonne above notified prices. By FY26, that premium had fallen to approximately ₹275 per tonne. This meant that even though MCL was dispatching more coal, it was earning considerably less from each tonne sold through auctions. 
 The lesson here is fairly important: MCL may control how efficiently it mines coal, but its realisations are influenced by Coal India's pricing decisions and the prevailing demand-supply situation.
 That said, even with softer realisations, MCL remains an exceptionally profitable mining business. In FY26, it reported an EBITDA margin of 47.45% and a PAT margin of 31.56%, among the highest for Indian coal producers.
 Source: Mahanadi Coalfields Ltd RHP In other words, MCL generated substantial profits (over ₹10,698 cr) with debt of just ₹3.16 cr as of March 2026. Its operational efficiency gives it a considerable cushion even when coal prices and auction premiums are less favourable.
 But extracting coal efficiently is only half the job. Once it leaves the mine, it has to reach thermal power plants, steel mills, and other industrial customers. And for a company producing more than 200 million tonnes annually, transportation can become a major bottleneck. Traditionally, a significant portion of MCL's coal moved by road, which can be slower and more expensive, particularly over long distances.
 That's gradually changing. Rail accounted for 65.28% of MCL's dispatches in FY26, up from 58.70% in FY24, while road transportation fell to 30.74%. The company is also investing in First-Mile Connectivity infrastructure, including silos and rapid-loading systems that allow coal to be loaded directly onto trains. Over 96% of dispatches through this infrastructure are rail-based. Essentially, instead of loading coal onto trucks, moving it to a railway siding and then transferring it again, the company is trying to create a more direct route from the mine to the train.
 MCL also has access to five seaports, which alone handle around 21.5% of its dispatches. This is particularly useful because it allows the company to supply coastal power plants that might otherwise depend on imported coal. Better rail and port connectivity could therefore help MCL reach more customers while reducing transportation friction. In a business where margins depend on moving enormous quantities of a relatively low-value commodity, efficient logistics can be just as important as mining efficiency.
 However, there are a few less obvious risks investors need to consider. 
 For starters, MCL depends heavily on a relatively small group of customers. Its top 10 customers accounted for 55.94% of revenue in FY26. That means if a few large power producers reduce purchases, switch suppliers or develop alternative sources of fuel, MCL could feel the impact.
 Competition could also change over time. India's coal reforms have encouraged private companies to develop commercial coal mines, while several large industrial buyers are developing captive coal blocks to secure their own fuel supplies. If these mines become operational and start supplying more coal, they could reduce some of the demand MCL currently enjoys through long-term supply agreements. The threat may not be immediate, given MCL's scale and established customer relationships, but it is something investors should keep an eye on over the longer term.
 And finally, there is the energy transition. India may continue depending on coal for years, but renewable energy capacity is expanding. If solar, wind and battery storage become increasingly competitive, the economics of coal-fired power generation could gradually change. MCL's enormous resource base is certainly an advantage, but having coal underground doesn't automatically mean all of it will remain commercially viable to extract and sell.
 Which brings us to what the Mahanadi Coalfields IPO is really about. On the operational front, MCL has several things going for it. It has enormous coal reserves, highly mechanised mining operations, industry-leading labour productivity, excellent profitability and very little debt. Its investments in rail connectivity and first-mile infrastructure could also help it overcome one of the biggest bottlenecks in the coal business.
 But we shouldn't mistake an efficient mining operation for a business with complete pricing freedom. Much of MCL's coal is sold at prices notified by Coal India, and a meaningful portion of its profitability depends on the premiums it earns through e-auctions.
 There's also an important distinction in what this IPO achieves. MCL isn't raising fresh capital to expand its operations. Coal India is selling a 10% stake in its subsidiary to unlock value from a business that was previously buried within the larger group. For investors, the listing offers an opportunity to own one of India's most productive and profitable coal companies directly. But it also forces them to think about how long the underlying business can remain attractive.
 After all, MCL has enough reserves to sustain production for decades, and further conversion of geological resources into mineable reserves could extend that horizon considerably. But the real question isn't whether MCL has enough coal. It is whether India will continue needing that coal at the same scale, and whether MCL can maintain its exceptional economics as the country’s energy mix is actively moving away from coal.
 Until then…
